title: Martinson & Berridge (2015): Multiple-Choice Quiz
instructions: Choose the single best answer. Distinguish the review's categories of proposed remedies, findings from individual cited studies, and the normative arguments made by critics and reviewers. No single cultural or health profile defines a person's worth.

items.prompt: What contribution did Villar attribute to the Rowe–Kahn model, as summarized in the introduction?
options: It stimulated interest in biological, behavioral, and social influences and a preventive, optimistic view of later life.
It restricted research to biological causes of disease and discouraged attention to behavioral or social influences.
It established one universally accepted definition of successful aging and ended conceptual disagreement in the field.
It removed social engagement from the criteria and replaced it with a purely clinical assessment of physical health.
items.answer: It stimulated interest in biological, behavioral, and social influences and a preventive, optimistic view of later life.
items.explanation: The introduction acknowledges Villar's positive assessment before reviewing the criticisms. It also emphasizes the continuing absence of an agreed definition. Recognizing the model's influence is distinct from accepting all of its criteria or dismissing the concerns examined in this review.

items.prompt: Why did the authors choose the Abstracts in Social Gerontology database?
options: It limited the search to biological and psychological studies, excluding cultural and critical gerontology.
It offered a broad interdisciplinary range of social-gerontology research.
It supplied empirical studies only, ensuring that theoretical analyses and editorials could not enter the review.
It comprehensively included every relevant book and all non-English critiques of successful-aging models.
items.answer: It offered a broad interdisciplinary range of social-gerontology research.
items.explanation: ASG provided biological, psychological, sociological, economic, cultural, and critical research. The review selected 67 articles in which critique was central, including empirical work, theoretical analyses, and editorials. The database choice was a scope decision, not a claim to cover all relevant scholarship.

items.prompt: What did the cited McLaughlin follow-up study find when it progressively relaxed successful-aging criteria?
options: An unchanged prevalence of 11.9% under every version of the criteria.
A narrow range of 16%–24% that remained almost unchanged by the revisions.
A decrease from 33.5% to 3.3% as the criteria became progressively less restrictive.
A prevalence range of 3.3%–33.5%, depending on how restrictive the criteria were.
items.answer: A prevalence range of 3.3%–33.5%, depending on how restrictive the criteria were.
items.explanation: The review reports this range from the cited follow-up, illustrating sensitivity to definitions. The investigators recommended loosening thresholds while retaining the Rowe–Kahn foundation. These are results of a particular reviewed study, not a pooled prevalence estimate from the 67-article review or a universal rate.

items.prompt: What did Villar propose adding when revising a successful-aging framework?
options: A stricter requirement to avoid every disease and disability.
A single self-rating that would completely replace all other dimensions.
A biomedical index combining marital status with leisure frequency.
A multifaceted concept of generativity alongside maintenance and loss regulation.
items.answer: A multifaceted concept of generativity alongside maintenance and loss regulation.
items.explanation: Villar proposed including generativity involving personal, community, and social development. The review presents this as a recommendation for revising a model, not an intervention result demonstrating that one new criterion resolves the broader objections to normative ideals.

items.prompt: What most clearly distinguishes Missing Voices from Add and Stir?
options: It only lowers thresholds set by experts, without seeking older adults' own accounts.
It gathers older adults' views but explicitly excludes them from the criteria or measures.
It specifically calls for criteria derived from older adults' own subjective meanings.
It removes subjective experience and replaces it with more detailed biomedical categories.
items.answer: It specifically calls for criteria derived from older adults' own subjective meanings.
items.explanation: Both groups criticize narrow criteria and largely retain successful aging as an ideal. Missing Voices is distinguished by explicitly grounding additional criteria in older adults' perspectives. The review sorts articles by their proposed remedies, even when the concerns they express overlap.
items.source: Categories: whose meanings shape the criteria

items.prompt: Which comparison did Strawbridge and colleagues report, according to the review?
options: 63% self-rated success versus 30% meeting the Rowe–Kahn criteria.
50.3% self-rated success versus 18.8% meeting the Rowe–Kahn criteria.
18.8% self-rated success versus 50.3% meeting the Rowe–Kahn criteria.
50.3% under both measures, with no difference between the definitions.
items.answer: 50.3% self-rated success versus 18.8% meeting the Rowe–Kahn criteria.
items.explanation: The review attributes 50.3% versus 18.8% to Strawbridge and colleagues. The 63% versus 30% comparison belongs to a different study involving African American older adults. The findings illustrate how subjective and externally defined classifications can differ; they do not rank either group's worth or establish one population-wide percentage.
items.source: Reviewed evidence: self-ratings and external criteria

items.prompt: What did Torres's intracultural approach show about meanings of successful aging?
options: Each culture determines one fixed definition shared by all its members.
Migration removes all influence of earlier cultural values on later-life meanings.
Definitions and the values behind them vary both across and within cultures.
Cultural values necessarily lead every member toward an identical understanding.
items.answer: Definitions and the values behind them vary both across and within cultures.
items.explanation: Torres examined complexity among people migrating between cultural settings and emphasized variation in both definitions and how people reach them. Cultural values can guide interpretation without dictating one position for every person. Culture-specific labels should therefore not become stereotypes that erase differences within a group.
items.source: Culture: variation within as well as between groups

items.prompt: What distinguishes the overall direction of Hard Hitting Critiques?
options: They retain the model and respond only by lowering the existing biomedical thresholds.
They preserve every original assumption while changing only the name to an Eastern ideal.
They challenge the broader ideal and seek alternatives addressing exclusion and structural injustice.
They accept the model unchanged except for adding a single subjective self-rating question.
items.answer: They challenge the broader ideal and seek alternatives addressing exclusion and structural injustice.
items.explanation: These critiques raise one or more concerns about individualism, ageism, ableism, neoliberal contexts, lived experience, and social justice. Their broad rejection of the successful-aging ideal distinguishes them from modest expansion. The category summarizes related arguments; it does not imply that every article makes every criticism.
items.source: Categories: fundamental criticism and alternative directions

items.prompt: What did Scheidt and colleagues argue was missing from an individualistic account of successful aging?
options: The powerful role of social and structural contexts in shaping how people age.
The claim that a positive individual attitude can always offset unequal opportunities.
The value of classifying every person as a winner or loser at one fixed endpoint.
The principle that physical-function scores make social circumstances irrelevant.
items.answer: The powerful role of social and structural contexts in shaping how people age.
items.explanation: The review attributes this critique to Scheidt and colleagues and connects it with unequal access to education, employment, housing, food, and other resources. It challenges explanations centered solely on individual control. This is an argument about how aging should be understood, not a numerical estimate of one structural cause.

items.prompt: What moral consequence did critics identify in defining success as avoiding disease and disability?
options: It can devalue people with illness or disability as failures and assign them personal blame.
It necessarily elevates disabled people above nondisabled people in a hierarchy of success.
It eliminates all comparisons of capacity and protects people from every moral judgment.
It guarantees equal social standing by placing every health condition in the highest category.
items.answer: It can devalue people with illness or disability as failures and assign them personal blame.
items.explanation: The critics argue that apparently neutral success language can create hierarchies of bodies and moral responsibility. The review examines this stigmatizing potential; it does not endorse the judgment that illness or disability makes a life unsuccessful. The proposed response values diversity, interdependence, and dignity.

items.prompt: Which policy proposals did Holstein and Minkler warn could lose support under stereotypes of self-sufficient successful agers?
options: Reducing coverage for home adaptations and assistive devices while freezing income support.
Expanding home adaptations while permanently capping income support below the poverty line.
Shifting device costs onto recipients and replacing material income support with health advice.
Expanding coverage for adaptations and assistive devices, and raising income support above poverty.
items.answer: Expanding coverage for adaptations and assistive devices, and raising income support above poverty.
items.explanation: The quoted criticism argues that portraying older people as needing little public support may weaken support for these expansions. It is a historical policy argument cited in the review, not a claim that the review measured an enacted funding cut or a statement of current program coverage.

items.prompt: What expectations were associated with the spunky-survivorship narrative discussed in the review?
options: A clinical rule requiring physicians to determine recurrence risk before discussing emotional concerns.
Positive thinking, health-promoting behavior, and pressure not to identify with frailty.
A requirement to identify with frailty and express fear in order to count as a successful survivor.
A formal support-group rule guaranteeing that every participant could express discomfort without judgment.
items.answer: Positive thinking, health-promoting behavior, and pressure not to identify with frailty.
items.explanation: The reviewed study described how these expectations could burden women who had experienced breast cancer, leaving less room for fear or discomfort and framing recurrence as personal failure. This is a critique of a moralizing narrative, not advice about how a person with cancer ought to feel or evidence that attitude determines recurrence.
items.source: Lived experience: pressures of a survivor ideal

items.prompt: Which response fits the social-justice-oriented recommendations?
options: Make housing and income support conditional on compliance with standardized exercise and diet rules.
Strengthen economic security, safe housing, protection from discrimination, and respect for dignity.
Make freedom from disease the sole policy goal and restrict community work to teaching self-management.
Leave economic and housing conditions unchanged while addressing every difficulty through individual counseling.
items.answer: Strengthen economic security, safe housing, protection from discrimination, and respect for dignity.
items.explanation: The critics call for policy, institutional, and community strategies that address material conditions and discrimination. They also emphasize older adults' own needs, meanings, and rights to self-determination, including people with disability or illness. The review synthesizes these recommendations rather than testing a specific policy package.
items.source: Social justice: conditions that support dignity

items.prompt: How does Wild and colleagues' ecological account broaden resilience?
options: It includes individual–social interdependence, power inequalities, and often overlooked community resources.
It confines resilience to positive attitude and coping while placing social structure outside the model.
It equates resilience with avoiding disease and dependence, excluding local resources from consideration.
It separates individuals from their communities and assumes one uniform meaning across all cultures.
items.answer: It includes individual–social interdependence, power inequalities, and often overlooked community resources.
items.explanation: The review highlights an approach incorporating older adults' meanings, structural conditions, power, and hidden resources in marginalized communities. It also cautions that resilience language can be used to blame people. This ecological example goes beyond the mainly individual focus of many alternative ideals in New Frames and Names.

items.prompt: Which limitation did the authors identify about the review's coverage?
options: Only biomedical ASG studies were selected, excluding theoretical and cultural critiques by design.
Only theoretical analyses and editorials were selected, excluding all critiques based on empirical work.
Scholarship outside ASG and non-English critiques, including less individualistic perspectives, may be missing.
Only non-English sources were reviewed, leaving English-language critiques of aging and individualism unexamined.
items.answer: Scholarship outside ASG and non-English critiques, including less individualistic perspectives, may be missing.
items.explanation: The review was restricted to English-language articles in ASG. Relevant books, work in other disciplinary journals, and other languages could therefore be absent. The 67 included articles support a configurative synthesis within this search scope, not a complete census of every critique or culture.
items.source: Limitations: search scope and missing perspectives
